description.shortText: AI software that supports legal prosecutions by automatically detecting and enforcing sentences. The Internet of Things would feed nearly unhackable data into the system to ensure informed decision-making while addressing law-breaking.

attachments.name: How has the law been pushed aside in the age of AI?
attachments.description: AI and automation in general are responsible for an increasing number of decisions by public authorities worldwide, however current ‘AI ethics’ usually removes these technologies from legal accountability.

attachments.name: Weapons of Math Destruction
attachments.description: Weapons of Math Destruction is a 2016 book about the societal impact of algorithms, written by Cathy O'Neil. It explores how some big data algorithms are increasingly used in ways that reinforce preexisting inequality.

attachments.name: The accuracy, fairness, and limits of predicting recidivism
attachments.description: Algorithms for predicting recidivism are commonly used to assess a criminal defendant’s likelihood of committing a crime. These predictions are used in pretrial, parole, and sentencing decisions. Proponents of these systems argue that big data and advanced machine learning make these analyses more accurate and less biased than humans. We show, however, that the widely used commercial risk assessment software COMPAS is no more accurate or fair than predictions made by people with little or no criminal justice expertise. In addition, despite COMPAS’s collection of 137 features, the same accuracy can be achieved with a simple linear classifier with only two features.

attachments.name: Police in California and Texas Test Networked Guns
attachments.description: A chip that tracks how a police officer’s gun is being used could prove useful in investigations and court cases.

attachments.name: A Popular Crime-Predicting Algorithms Performed Worse Than Mechanical Turks in One Study
attachments.description: When researchers put a popular criminal justice algorithm up against a bunch of Mechanical Turks, they came out about even.

attachments.name: UK police are using AI to make custodial decisions – but it could be discriminating against the poor
attachments.description: Durham Constabulary, which has been testing its HART algorithm since 2017, recently made changes to avoid reinforcing human biases against people living in certain areas

attachments.name: Correctional Offender Management Profiles for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) (Pages:49-75)
attachments.description:
"Correctional Offender Management Profiles for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS)" is the chapter of a book called "Handbook of Recidivism Risk/Needs Assessment Tools, First Edition" written by Tim Brennan and William Dieterich. 
The chapter describes the COMPAS system, as weel as the technical and non-technical values behind the software developed and owned by a company called Northpointe, now kwon as Equivant.

attachments.name: Helping police make custody decisions using artificial intelligence
attachments.description: Police at the “front line” of difficult risk-based judgements are trialling an AI system trained by University of Cambridge criminologists to give guidance using the outcomes of five years of criminal histories.

attachments.name: Facewatch, the greatest advance in security since the introduction of CCTV.
attachments.description: Facewatch is a secure cloud-based platform that uses facial recognition technology to send instant alerts when subjects of interest enter business premises.  We proactively deter and protect businesses against crime. It is the ONLY shared national facial recognition watchlist.

attachments.name: COMPAS (software) - Wikipedia
attachments.description: COMPAS, an acronym for Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions, is a decision assistant software developed and owned by a company called Equivant (formally known as Northpointe) and used by U.S. courts to assess the probability of a defendant becoming a recidivist - influencing their right to a parole.

attachments.name: Security Digital Platform
attachments.description: Security management platform addressing operator requirements, processing data from thousands of surveillance sensors aiming to improve security systems.

attachments.name: Ekin: Smart Patrol in a Lightbar
attachments.description: One product could allow a patrol to automatically check license plates, recognize faces, and speed and parking violations. Ekin's Patrol G2 is designed to do give AI policing capabilities to any patrolling car.

attachments.name: The Global Expansion of AI Surveillance
attachments.description: An increasing number of states are deploying advanced AI surveillance tools to monitor, track, and surveil citizens to accomplish a range of policy objectives - some are fair, others might violate human rights, and many fall into a complicated middle ground.

attachments.name: Inspector gadget: how smart devices are outsmarting criminals
attachments.description: Fitbits, pacemakers, Amazon Echoes – all are tools of the modern detective’s trade in a world where our devices are always watching
